subject: Switzerland
note: Cited to one pinned Wikipedia revision (trusted_secondary): Büsingen am Hochrhein. The page gives the area twice (7.62 km2 and 762 hectares, the same) and the population as 'about 1,548' and 'around 1,540'; a script uses 7.62 km2 and 'about 1,548'. Natural Earth does not draw this 7.6 km2 exclave, so the map shows a marker at the page's infobox coordinate and never an outline; captions do not claim the border is drawn. The page gives no coordinates for Dörflingen or Stemmer, so neither is marked.

claims.text: Büsingen is an exclave of Germany and Baden-Württemberg, and an enclave of Switzerland, entirely surrounded by the Swiss cantons of Schaffhausen, Zürich, and Thurgau.
Büsingen is a German municipality of 7.62 km2 in the south of Baden-Württemberg with a population of about 1,548 inhabitants.
It is separated from the rest of Germany by a narrow strip of land (at its narrowest, about 680 m wide) containing the Swiss village of Dörflingen.
Politically Büsingen is part of Germany, but economically it forms part of the Swiss customs union; there have been no border controls between Switzerland and Büsingen since 4 October 1967.
The Swiss VAT applies to purchases made in Büsingen, at a rate of 7.7% compared with general German VAT at 19%.
Büsingen is the only German village in which people pay mostly with Swiss francs, although officially the euro is legal tender.
In 1918 a referendum was held in Büsingen in which 96% of voters voted to become part of Switzerland; no land transfer took place as Switzerland could not offer anything suitable in exchange.
Its border with Switzerland is 17.141 kilometres long and is marked by 123 stones.
Büsingen has its own licence plate (BÜS), and there are only around 700 in use at any one time.
The local football team, FC Büsingen, is the only German team to play in the Swiss Football League.
